result: Viral-mediated expression of GCaMP in cerebellar molecular layer interneurons (MLIs) was achieved with high specificity and efficiency. Using AAV2/1 or AAV2/9 with the human synapsin promoter resulted in almost exclusive GECI expression in MLI somata and neurites, with over 90% of MLIs expressing GECI by 7 days post-injection, and expression levels increasing over the first 2 weeks.
evaluation: Claims C1-C3 are well-supported by immunohistochemical data (Figure 1B), temporal expression analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), and citations to prior work validating this approach. The quantitative data on expression efficiency (>90%) and time course provide strong evidence for the technical success of the method.

result: Parallel fiber (PF) stimulation evokes calcium transients in MLIs that increase with train duration. High frequency PF stimulation generated robust calcium rises with characteristic beam-shaped fluorescence patterns, with ΔF/Fo values increasing from 138.9 ± 30.6% for 0.2 s trains to 347 ± 43% for 1 s trains (N=18).
evaluation: Claims C4-C5 are supported by direct imaging data (Figure 1C-E) showing dose-response relationships with adequate sample size (N=18). The beam-shaped pattern is consistent with known PF anatomy and prior work (Sullivan et al., 2005).

result: mGluR1 receptors contribute significantly to PF-evoked calcium signals in MLIs in vivo, with the contribution depending on stimulation duration and frequency. CPCCOEt (mGluR1 antagonist) significantly reduced somatic calcium signals, with the remaining signal abolished by iGluR antagonists. The mGluR1 contribution increased with train duration (minimal at 100 ms, ~50% at 1 s) and required high frequency (500 Hz for 100 ms trains). Similar mGluR1 contributions were observed in vivo and in slices.
evaluation: Claims C6-C12 are well-supported by systematic pharmacological experiments with appropriate controls (Figure 2). The dose-response relationships for train duration and frequency are quantified with statistical analysis (p-values provided). The comparison between in vivo and slice preparations strengthens the findings. Sequential drug application (C8) provides mechanistic insight into receptor contributions.

result: MLI calcium signals during locomotion in awake mice are partially mediated by mGluR1. Many MLIs showed fluorescence dynamics correlated with locomotion (ΔF/Frest peak values of 128.2 ± 8.5%, 313 ROIs from 4 mice). Linear regression analysis revealed a negative correlation (-0.547, R²=0.3, p<0.0001) between pre-drug fluorescence amplitude and the effect of CPCCOEt, indicating that larger calcium signals are more likely to involve mGluR1.
evaluation: Claims C13-C15 are supported by awake imaging data from 313 ROIs across 4 animals with appropriate statistical analysis. The correlation analysis (C15) provides quantitative evidence linking signal amplitude to mGluR1 involvement. However, the modest R² value (0.3) indicates substantial unexplained variance, and the forced locomotion paradigm may not fully represent natural behavior.

result: Ionotropic glutamate receptors (iGluRs) are essential for PF-evoked calcium rises in MLIs. Combined AMPAR and NMDAR blockade (GYKI53655 + DCK) strongly decreased calcium signals across all train durations tested, blocking 94% of the response to 1 s, 100 Hz trains (ratio 0.06 ± 0.01).
evaluation: Claims C16-C17 are supported by pharmacological data from both in vivo and slice experiments (Figure 4A-B). The near-complete block (94%) by iGluR antagonists provides strong evidence for their necessity. Sample sizes are adequate (n=6 per condition).

result: AMPARs in adult MLIs lack calcium permeability. IEM1460 (CP-AMPAR blocker) had no effect on PF-evoked calcium signals in vivo, and all MLIs tested (n=7) showed linear I-V relations characteristic of calcium-impermeable AMPARs. This represents a developmental switch from juvenile to adult, as CP-AMPARs have been reported in young animals.
evaluation: Claims C18-C19 are well-supported by converging pharmacological (IEM1460) and electrophysiological (I-V curves) evidence. The sample size for electrophysiology is modest (n=7) but adequate for this type of measurement. Claim C20 is appropriately supported by citations to prior work showing similar developmental changes in other brain regions.

result: mGluR1-mediated calcium signals require voltage-gated calcium channels (VGCCs). Glutamate uncaging-evoked calcium rises were mediated by mGluR1 (blocked by CPCCOEt) and were strongly reduced by CdCl2 (VGCC blocker), with peak ΔF/Fo decreasing from 438 ± 47% to 6 ± 2% (n=4). This indicates that iGluRs act on mGluR1 responses via VGCCs.
evaluation: Claims C21-C23 are supported by glutamate uncaging experiments with pharmacological manipulations. The dramatic effect of CdCl2 (>98% reduction) provides strong evidence for VGCC involvement. However, the sample size for the CdCl2 experiment is small (n=4), which limits confidence in the precise quantitative estimates.

result: mGluR1α receptors are localized perisynaptically at PF-MLI synapses, positioned for synergistic interactions with AMPARs. Freeze-fracture electron microscopy revealed that mGluR1α has highest density within 50 nm of the synapse edge. Prior work established that mGluR1α is expressed in all cerebellar GABAergic neurons while other mGluR1 isoforms are absent from MLIs.
evaluation: Claims C24-C27 are supported by quantitative electron microscopy (Figure 6C) and appropriate citations to prior immunohistochemical work. The spatial distribution data directly supports the interpretation of functional synergy (C27). The EM analysis was replicated across multiple animals (mentioned in Figure 6C legend).

result: The study demonstrates three main findings: (1) mGluR1s are activated in vivo by synaptically-released glutamate during both electrical stimulation and locomotion, with contribution increasing sharply with train duration; (2) mGluR1s and iGluRs act synergistically to produce calcium rises; (3) the spatial distribution of receptors at PF-MLI synapses favors homosynaptic iGluR/mGluR1 synergy. High frequency PF activity resembling physiological patterns engages mGluR1s in an iGluR-dependent manner.
evaluation: Claims C28-C32 represent summary statements of the major findings, each supported by the detailed experimental results described in previous claim groups. The convergence of pharmacological, imaging, and anatomical evidence provides strong support for these conclusions. The reference to physiologically relevant activity patterns (C32, citing Jörntell and Ekerot, 2006) strengthens the biological relevance.

result: The current work demonstrates direct mGluR1 activation at PF-MLI synapses with fast kinetics (<1 s latency), contrasting with prior in vivo observations that may have been indirect (>10 s latency). This suggests mGluR1 activation in vivo may be widespread across different synapse types and activity patterns, even at synapses lacking glial ensheathing elements.
evaluation: Claims C33-C34 appropriately contextualize the current findings relative to prior work (Wang et al., 2011), with the faster kinetics supporting direct activation. Claim C35 is a reasonable generalization based on the finding that mGluR1 activation occurs at PF-MLI synapses despite their lack of glial ensheathment, though it remains somewhat speculative regarding other synapse types.

result: MLI activation during locomotion is consistent with the functional anatomy of cerebellar lobule IV/V and prior studies. During locomotion, 94% of granule cells are activated, MLI firing increases from 20 Hz to 60 Hz, and granule cells fire in high-frequency bursts (60-142 Hz, 30-140 ms duration). These physiological parameters closely match those required for mGluR1 activation in the electrical stimulation experiments.
evaluation: Claims C36-C40 appropriately integrate the current findings with prior literature on cerebellar functional anatomy and physiology. The citations to prior work (Provini et al., 1968; Jelitai et al., 2016; Ozden et al., 2012; Jörntell and Ekerot, 2006) support the contextual claims. The comparison between physiological activity patterns and experimental stimulation parameters (C40) strengthens the biological relevance of the findings.

result: The synergy between iGluRs and mGluR1 functions as a nonlinear switch controlling plasticity at PF-MLI synapses. High frequency or prolonged PF activity induces strong calcium rises through this synergy, which gates plasticity and governs MLI inhibitory output. The correlation between mGluR1 block extent and calcium rise amplitude may reflect different PF activity patterns during behavior.
evaluation: Claims C41-C42 are supported by the experimental data showing synergistic interactions. However, claim C43 regarding the "nonlinear switch" controlling plasticity is speculative, as no plasticity experiments were performed. The functional role in "gating plasticity" and "governing inhibition output" represents interpretation beyond the direct evidence, which focused on calcium signaling rather than synaptic plasticity or inhibitory function.

result: The mechanism of iGluR/mGluR1 synergy involves AMPAR-mediated depolarization activating VGCCs, which initiates calcium rise and enables mGluR1 responses. AMPARs alone (not NMDARs) are responsible for the synergy, as demonstrated by sequential pharmacological experiments showing that NMDAR blockade does not affect CPCCOEt-insensitive signals.
evaluation: Claims C44-C47 are supported by converging pharmacological evidence from both cited prior work (Collin et al., 2009) and current experiments. The sequential drug application experiments (Figure 2C, claim C47) provide clear evidence that AMPARs rather than NMDARs mediate the synergy. The mechanistic interpretation (C46) is well-supported by the VGCC dependence data.

result: The AMPAR/mGluR1 synergy constitutes a "double key system" controlling postsynaptic calcium responses, analogous to the AMPAR/NMDAR requirement for long-term plasticity at other synapses. This is consistent with prior findings at PF-PC synapses and may involve calcium-dependent phospholipase C as a mechanistic basis for synergy.
evaluation: Claims C48 and C50-C51 appropriately contextualize the findings within established synaptic plasticity mechanisms, with C48 supported by citation to prior work on Purkinje cells (Okubo et al., 2004). Claim C49 regarding phospholipase C is appropriately presented as speculative ("plausible source") with citation to supporting work (Kim et al., 2011). The analogy to AMPAR/NMDAR interactions is conceptually sound.

result: Despite lacking NMDARs at the synapse (though present extrasynaptically), PF-MLI synapses exhibit various forms of plasticity. The combined activation of AMPARs and mGluR1s could control postsynaptic calcium signals responsible for associative plasticity, similar to AMPAR/NMDAR interactions elsewhere. This parallels mechanisms in hippocampal interneurons requiring mGluR1, CP-AMPARs, and T-type calcium channels.
evaluation: Claims C52-C54 are well-supported by citations to prior electrophysiological work. However, claim C55 is speculative ("could control") as no plasticity experiments were performed in this study. The hypothesis is reasonable by analogy to other systems (C56), but remains untested. The functional role in plasticity requires experimental validation.

result: An alternative mechanism for iGluR/mGluR synergy involving electrical field effects on glutamate escape is unlikely to fully account for the observed synergy, because the synergy depends on calcium influx rather than just glutamate concentration dynamics.
evaluation: Claims C57-C58 appropriately acknowledge an alternative mechanism from prior work (Sylantyev et al., 2013) while providing reasoning for why it cannot fully explain the current findings. The logic that calcium-dependence argues against a purely electrical field mechanism is sound, though the authors appropriately note they cannot completely exclude this possibility.

result: Comparison of mGluR1 distribution between PF-PC and PF-MLI synapses reveals similar perisynaptic localization despite morphological differences. Both synapse types show ~50% of mGluR1α within 60 nm of the synapse edge, consistent with homosynaptic activation. PF-MLI synapses have smaller PSDs (favoring homosynaptic signaling) but lack glial ensheathment (favoring spillover), with the shorter distance to receptors apparently overruling the lack of glial barrier.
evaluation: Claims C59-C67 integrate current EM findings with prior anatomical knowledge and literature. The quantitative comparison between PF-PC and PF-MLI receptor distributions (C61-C62) is supported by appropriate citations. The interpretation weighing competing factors (C67) is reasonable based on the spatial distribution data, though somewhat speculative. The anatomical claims (C59-C60) represent established knowledge appropriately cited.

result: The temporal requirements for mGluR1 activation reflect receptor kinetics. Due to slow activation and low desensitization, single releases activate few mGluR1s, but high-frequency bursts recruit sufficient receptors. Longer trains increasingly recruit mGluR1s as AMPARs desensitize. In vivo, mGluR1-mediated calcium rises begin at ~100 ms burst duration (physiologically relevant), though the actual threshold may be lower due to GCaMP limitations.
evaluation: Claims C68-C74 integrate biophysical receptor properties (C68, established knowledge) with experimental observations. The temporal threshold determination (C73) is supported by experimental data (Figure 2) and appropriately contextualized with physiological activity patterns. The caveat about GCaMP limitations (C74) is appropriate scientific caution. Citations to prior slice work (C70) support the interpretation.
